title: Degraded-mode tiered failover protocol
content:
Purpose:

This doc proposes a pragmatic, multi-tiered approach to keep inference serving available with graceful quality degradation when resource constraints, kernel regressions, or transient failures occur. The goal is to define deterministic per-request downgrade paths, an orchestrable controller that coordinates kernel/model/scheduling fallbacks, and a KV-cache treatment that preserves downstream correctness without causing cascading OOMs.

Scope:
- Applies to the hosted and dedicated runtime (private deployments opt-in).
- Covers per-request decision flow (fast path -> degraded paths), kernel downgrade manager behavior, model-proxy Plan-B, KV cache eviction/checkpointing, retry and circuit breaker semantics.
- Does NOT replace higher-level routing policies (region routing, customer tiering) but integrates with them.

Motivation / Observed failure modes:
- Sudden memory pressure (e.g., larger-than-expected sequence length) can trigger multi-tenant OOMs and runtime restarts.
- Kernel regression (introduced by new optimized op) can cause elevated per-request latency or silent memory growth for certain model shims.
- Backpressure (slow GPUs) combined with aggressive batching leads to request pileups and increased tail latency.
- Naive global kv-eviction can remove prefixes used by many warm sessions, causing thundering cache-misses and load spikes.

Design goals (priority):
1) Fast, predictable per-request downgrade decisions (< 1 ms decision budget).
2) Bounded memory impact under pressure; avoid full-host eviction cascades.
3) Preserve best-effort quality: prefer quantized/shorter-context alternatives over outright rejection.
4) Observability: every downgrade path must emit a clear metric/log and attach context to traces.
5) Safe rollback: rollouts of downgrade logic should be toggleable by feature-flags and per-deployment config.

High-level approach (tiered failover):
- Tier 0: Full-quality path (native kernel, pinned full model, standard KV lookup, normal batching)
- Tier 1: Kernel-reduced path (use safe, conservative kernel variant: no experimental fused ops; smaller workspace allocations)
- Tier 2: Model-lite path (serve a lower-footprint model variant or quantized clone, same tokenizer)
- Tier 3: Context-trimmed path (truncate or summarize input prefix; use prefix-only cache hits)
- Tier 4: Proxy plan-B (stateless lightweight response generator + user-facing degrade message)
- Terminal: Reject (only when all prior tiers fail or when governed by explicit SLA/canary policy)

Components:

1) Degradation Controller (DC)
- A per-host, low-latency decision service co-located with request router.
- Inputs: current host memory pressure, kernel health score, queue depth, tenant QoS, model pin status, KV cache hit ratios, per-request flags (pin_to_full, require_exact).
- Outputs: per-request tier assignment and a short eviction hint for KV manager.
- Implementation note: keep it single-threaded and lock-free for reads; update periodic state from SRE agents (every 250ms).

2) Kernel Downgrade Manager (KDM)
- Maintains a set of kernel variants labeled stable/conservative/experimental.
- On Tier 1 activation, swap kernel ABI pointers for new requests only; avoid preempting running kernels in the middle of exec.
- Health probes: synthetic microbenchmarks that run on a spare GPU core and report latency/memory delta. KDM increments a degradation score when probes cross thresholds.

3) Model Proxy (Plan-B)
- Stateless microservice that returns one of: cached stub responses, short-form extraction, or a templated fallback message (e.g., "estimated reply delayed; try again") depending on tenant policy.
- Must never persist user data. For enterprise customers with strict SLOs we prefer model-lite over Plan-B.
- Operational toggle: per-customer opt-out via entitlement flag.

4) KV Cache micro-checkpointing and staged eviction
- Problem: global LRU eviction causes correlated cache misses for many sessions.
- Proposal: add two mechanisms: micro-checkpoints and staged eviction windows.
  - Micro-checkpoints: periodically snapshot hot prefixes (partial KV states) to local SSD if memory pressure looks imminent. Checkpoints are sharded by tenant and prefix-hash; they live no longer than 24h unless promoted.
  - Staged eviction: instead of evicting N items immediately, mark them as soft-evict with a 30–90s grace window. Requests that miss a soft-evicted key can rehydrate from checkpoint or request a read-through but are rate-limited by the DC to avoid stampedes.
- Eviction priority considers: (1) tenant QoS weight, (2) last-access age, (3) checkpoint availability.

5) Retry & Circuit Breakers
- Retries are split into local and global: local retries (within same host) are limited to 1 attempt and only for idempotent read ops. Global retries (routed to another host/model variant) are controlled by the DC and are discouraged for tail-sensitive workloads.
- Circuit breaker states: CLOSED, SOFT_OPEN (serve Tier 1/2 automatically), HARD_OPEN (immediate Plan-B or reject). Each circuit breaker is keyed by (tenant, model, kernel_variant).
- Transition triggers: error rate threshold, memory pressure spikes, probe failures. Backoff uses a clipped exponential capped at 30s.

6) Scheduler interplay and batching
- Batching scheduler must expose per-request priority and tier affinity. Lower-tier requests are eligible for delayed batching windows (longer batching TTL) to preserve capacity for Tier 0 requests.
- Prefer adaptive batching: when host enters degraded mode, reduce max batch size for Tier 0 to improve latency predictability and increase batching window for Tier 2/3 to preserve throughput.

Observability and tracing:
- Every degraded decision emits: host_id, request_id, assigned_tier, reason_code, mem_percent, kernel_variant, kv_action (none/checkpointed/soft-evict), correlating_trace_id.
- New metrics: degraded_requests_total (by tier), degradation_latency_p95, cache_rehydrate_rate, micro_checkpoint_size_bytes, soft_evict_stall_seconds, plan_b_invocations_total.
- Alerting: page when HARD_OPEN persists beyond 1m for > 5% of hosts running a model, or when Plan-B invocation rate > 2% global for 5m.

Safety, correctness and privacy considerations:
- Checkpoints on local SSD must be encrypted and ephemeral; do not include raw user tokens beyond minimal prefix hashes.
- Model-lite fallbacks should be functionally equivalent (same tokenizer) to avoid confusing downstream layers.
- For regulated tenants, Plan-B must be disabled by default; fallback path must choose a quantized private clone instead.

Rollout plan (canary -> gradual):
- Phase 0: Feature-flagged DC + KDM in dev environments; log-only mode for 2 weeks.
- Phase 1: Canary on ~1% hosted capacity; enable staged eviction + soft-evict behavior. Monitor metrics for cache stampede.
- Phase 2: Expand to 25% with Plan-B enabled for non-regulated tenants, enable kernel swap probes.
- Phase 3: Global, on by default; provide operator knobs for tenants.

Operational runbook (summary):
- If host enters HARD_OPEN: reduce host routing weight, trigger controlled drain, activate PVC GPU warm pool if available.
- If micro-checkpoint store filling > 80%: increase checkpoint TTL pruning, mark new checkpoints as ephemeral-only.
- If Plan-B rate spikes: inspect KDM probe errors and kernel variant deployments; roll kernel back if probe error rate > 10%.

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Checkpoint durability vs write amplification: how often to checkpoint hot prefixes without thrashing SSD? Proposed default: snapshot on a 2x increase in per-tenant active prefix count since last checkpoint or every 60s under pressure.
- How aggressive should kernel pre-emption be? We avoid preempting in-flight ops; that leaves a window where memory still climbs. Could we support preemptible kernel-alloc arenas?
- Tenant-specific policies: should DC learn tenant tolerance via online RL or stay rule-based? Start rule-based.

Implementation notes / TODOs:
- [ ] Implement fast in-memory DC interface (C++ ring buffer read, Rust shim for safety). (ENG-2421)
- [ ] Add kernel health probe harness and KDM swap API. (PR #678)
- [ ] Prototype micro-checkpoint format and checkpoint store eviction policy. (Spike: 2 wks)
- [ ] Add tracing keys for degradation events and extend console dashboards.

Appendix: quick check-list for reviewers
- Is the per-request decision path free of locks and <1ms?
- Does staged eviction prevent stampedes in our simulations?
- Are kernel swap and rollback atomic from the router's perspective?
- Is Plan-B opt-out clearly enforced for regulated tenants?

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider an "emergency tiny model" baked into the runtime binary for absolute last-resort replies (very small, distilled transformer).
- Add a low-cost ML scorer in DC that predicts request cost (expected token count * kv-miss-likelihood) to improve preemptive tier assignment.

References and previous work:
- Related drive docs: runtime-resilience-fallback-spec, opportunistic-throttling-and-fallback-ladder-spec (useful context but this design takes a different approach focused on staged eviction and plan-B proxy).
- Spike results (not attached): local simulation with 5 tenants showed 65% reduction in simultaneous cache rehydrates when staged eviction used.

End.
